harbour.title: Harbour
harbour.intro: A platform for car importers. Every job from collection abroad to handover in one place, live GPS on the way, and a portal in the importer's brand where the buyer follows their own car.

Problem.label: 01 — PROBLEM
Problem.text: Importers bring cars to Cyprus from the UK, Japan and further away. One car passes through collection, registration, road legs, a ferry and customs, with a different partner at every step. Teams ran this on spreadsheets, WhatsApp and phone calls. Buyers called every few days to ask where their car was, GPS trackers sat in a drawer with no record of which car they were in, and costs only added up once the margin was already gone. No tool covered the whole journey: CRMs held the buyers, fleet trackers held the GPS, and nothing joined the two.
Problem.hmw: How might we give an importer one place that shows where every car is and what needs doing today, and give the buyer the same answer without a phone call?
Problem.name: Problem

Research.label: 02 — SCOPE
stats: Screens, desktop and mobile, with every state
User flows mapped in FigJam, from sign-in to handover
Routes in the codebase, each matched to a screen
Sides of one product: the business app and the buyer portal
Research.finding: Main finding: an owner's first question in the morning is not how many jobs there are, but which car needs them today and where it is. A buyer only asks where their car is and when they get it. Both answers come from the same two things: the job's stage and its tracker.
Research.name: Research

Audience.label: 03 — AUDIENCE
Audience.intro: One workspace, two roles. The owner runs the business side; the buyer sees only their own car, under the importer's brand.

personas.name: Owner at the desk
texts: One board with what is late, what is arriving and which trackers went quiet.

personas.name: Owner on the road
texts: “I’m at the depot with the car and a tracker.”
Mark the car collected, scan the tracker and take photos from a phone.

personas.name: Buyer
texts: A clear stage, an expected date and photos, without calling anyone.

Audience.name: Audience

Journey map.label: 04 — JOURNEY MAP
Journey map.intro: One import from the owner's side: what they do, think and struggle with at each stage, and the design decision that answers it.

rows.label: DOING
cells: Adds the buyer and the car
Collects the car, fits a tracker
Hands over the keys, closes the job

rows.label: THINKING
cells: “What has this cost me so far?”

rows.label: PAIN POINT
cells: Calls to drivers for a position

rows.label: DESIGN RESPONSE
cells: Three-step New job with buyer search
Assign tracker inside Mark collected, QR on mobile
Live map and GPS alerts on the Board
Portal: stage, live position, photos, documents

Journey map.name: Journey map

Hypotheses.label: 05 — HYPOTHESES
Hypotheses.intro: Six bets behind the design, each with the metric that will show whether it works.
items: A Board that leads with late tasks, arrivals and GPS alerts gets problems handled the same day, faster than a list of every job.
Assigning the tracker inside Mark collected means no car leaves without a tracker on record.
Jobs in transit with no tracker
A branded portal with the stage, live position and photos cuts “where is my car” calls.
Routes with their own stages let one workspace run UK → Cyprus and Japan → Cyprus without workarounds.
Jobs running on a second route
Costs and charges on the job show the margin before the car arrives, not after.
Jobs with costs entered before handover
A phone version with QR scanning lets the owner record a collection on site instead of later at a desk.
Hypotheses.name: Hypotheses

Prioritisation.label: 06 — PRIORITISATION
Prioritisation.intro: Each bet placed by expected impact and the effort to build it. The Board, tracker assignment and the portal went first: they answer the two questions everyone asks.
Prioritisation.name: Prioritisation

Visitor flow.label: 07 — USER FLOWS
Visitor flow.intro: Eleven flows are drawn in FigJam and matched to screens. This is the core one: open a job, collect the car with a tracker, follow it on the map, move it through the route's stages and hand it over, while the buyer sees each step in the portal. The words on each arrow are the button the user presses.
Visitor flow.name: Visitor flow

Sitemap.label: 08 — SITEMAP
Sitemap.intro: The owner's app has six places in the sidebar; everything about one car lives in the job workspace, in six tabs. The buyer portal is a separate, much smaller app under the importer's brand.
Sitemap.name: Sitemap

Wireframes to UI.label: 09 — WIREFRAMES TO UI
Wireframes to UI.name: Wireframes to UI
Wireframes to UI.intro: The Board as a wireframe first, agreed with the team before any colour, then the final screen: what needs the owner today at the top, the next arriving car and GPS alerts on the same screen.

Solution.label: 10 — SOLUTION
notes: Tracker on record
Each job shows its tracker, who assigned it and when. The IMEI never reaches the buyer.
Planned and driven
A dotted line for the planned corridor, a solid one for where the car has actually been.
One next step
The status bar names the stage and offers one button for the next one: Move to At Greece.
The same journey for the buyer
The portal shows the route's stages in plain words, with the current leg highlighted.
A date up front
The expected arrival is the first thing the buyer reads, above the car.
Only what is shared
Photos, documents and updates appear only when the owner marks them visible.
Solution.name: Solution

Screens.label: 11 — SCREENS
Screens.intro: Key screens: the job workspace, the live map, a new job, money, routes, the buyer portal and a customer record.
Screens.name: Screens

Mobile.label: 12 — MOBILE
Mobile.intro: The owner's phone version: a dark header, content on a light sheet and a floating tab bar. Collection, tracker QR scan and photos happen where the car is.
Mobile.name: Mobile

What we measure.label: 13 — WHAT WE MEASURE
What we measure.intro: Six hypotheses across the journey. Targets are set before launch and tracked once the first importers are on the new version.
table: Jobs in transit with no tracker
Jobs running on a second route
What we measure.name: What we measure

Results.label: 14 — RESULTS
cols: Where it is now

140+ screens for the business app, the buyer portal and sign-in, on desktop and mobile, built on one set of tokens and components. Every screen is matched to its route in the code, so the team builds straight from the file.
What I would do next
Test the portal with buyers on one live route and compare status calls before and after. Then design notifications, once we know which updates buyers actually want.
Results.name: Results

strata.title: Strata
strata.intro: A multi-site CMS for any business that runs many websites from one place. Shared pages and journeys, each site in its own brand, and every change checked, signed off and reversible.

Problem.label: 01 — PROBLEM
Problem.name: Problem
Problem.text: Many businesses run the same content across many websites: partners, regions, franchises or brands. Each site looks different, but the pages, prices and questions are mostly the same. Today every change means touching every site by hand: a price updated on nine sites and forgotten on three, a broken link nobody sees until a customer does, and no clear answer to “what was live on this site last Tuesday?”
Problem.hmw: How might we let a team change a page once, see exactly which sites it reaches, and publish or roll back with confidence?

Research.label: 02 — SCOPE
Research.name: Research
stats: User flows, from sign-in to analytics
Branded sites running from one workspace in the designs
Research.finding: Main finding: editing words was never the hard part. The hard part was knowing which sites a change reaches, whether it is safe to go live, and how to get back if it is not.

Audience.label: 03 — AUDIENCE
Audience.name: Audience
Audience.intro: Three roles share one tool, whatever the business. Each gets a home screen built around what needs them today.

personas.name: Product managers
texts: “Is anything broken on a live site right now?”
One place that shows what needs them, across all sites.

personas.name: Content editors
texts: “I just need to change the prices.”
Edit the page as customers see it, with sections they can move.

personas.name: Site managers
texts: “This partner wants its own colours, not its own pages.”
A brand per site that changes the look, never the content.

Journey map.label: 04 — JOURNEY MAP
Journey map.name: Journey map
Journey map.intro: What a product team does, thinks and struggles with from a request to a live change, and the design decision that answers it.

rows.label: DOING
cells: Gets new prices to roll out

rows.label: THINKING

“Can I undo it if it goes wrong?”

rows.label: PAIN POINT

Hypotheses.label: 05 — HYPOTHESES
Hypotheses.name: Hypotheses
Hypotheses.intro: Six bets behind the design, each with the metric that will show whether it works.
items: A Home that lists only what needs you gets broken sites fixed faster than a dashboard of charts.
Showing “9 sites change, 3 stay” before publishing stops changes reaching the wrong site.
Checks that stop publishing (links, headings, picture descriptions) catch problems before customers do.
Bundling drafts into one release with sign-off replaces approval by email.
Measuring a brand from an existing website gets a new site live without a designer.
Time to launch a new site
Plain words — page, site, journey, release — make the tool usable without training.
Support questions in the first month

Prioritisation.label: 06 — PRIORITISATION
Prioritisation.name: Prioritisation
Prioritisation.intro: Each bet placed by expected impact and the effort to build it. Publishing, checks and releases went first: every other feature depends on them.

Visitor flow.label: 07 — USER FLOWS
Visitor flow.name: Visitor flow
Visitor flow.intro: Seventeen flows are drawn screen by screen in the Figma file. This is the core one: edit a page, preview it as a customer, fix what stops publishing, check which sites change, go live, and roll back if needed. The words on each arrow are the button the user presses.

Sitemap.label: 08 — SITEMAP
Sitemap.name: Sitemap
Sitemap.intro: After sign-in you pick a workspace (in the designs, a home insurance product). Every workspace has the same sections in the sidebar. Library and Sites are shared by all of its sites.

Wireframes to UI.label: 09 — WIREFRAMES TO UI
Wireframes to UI.name: Wireframes to UI
Wireframes to UI.intro: The Home layout as a wireframe, then the final screen: what needs you on the left, changes and sites on the right.

Solution.label: 10 — SOLUTION
Solution.name: Solution
notes: Reach before publishing
The review says how many sites change and which ones stay as they are, before anything goes live.
Site wording kept
If a site has its own wording, the review shows it is kept, so a shared change never overwrites it.
Checks passed
Links, headings and picture descriptions are checked on every publish.
Things to fix
A counter in the editor shows what still needs attention before the page can go live.
Stops publishing
Some problems block the release, such as a section with no heading.
Won’t stop publishing
Others are warnings. They stay visible, and an override needs a reason that is kept in History.

Screens.label: 11 — SCREENS
Screens.name: Screens
Screens.intro: Key screens: the page designer, journeys, publishing, site brands, releases, history and checks.

What we measure.label: 12 — WHAT WE MEASURE
What we measure.name: What we measure
What we measure.intro: Six hypotheses across five stages. Targets are set before launch and tracked once the first sites are live.
table: Time to launch a new site

Results.label: 13 — RESULTS
Results.name: Results
cols: Where it is now
All 17 flows are designed, from sign-in to journey analytics, on one design system. The CMS is being built from these screens.
What I would do next
Test the publish review with real editors in different kinds of business, then bring a site’s brand into Figma as variables and back, so designers and Strata share one source.

inner-glow.title: Inner Glow AI
inner-glow.intro: A mental health app that turns daily check-ins into one score people can understand, and gives a next step for every result.

Problem.label: 01 — PROBLEM
Problem.name: Problem
Problem.intro: People who want to look after their mental health usually start strong and stop after a week. Mood trackers collect data but don't explain it, meditation apps don't know how you feel today, and therapy is expensive with long waiting lists. The result is a lot of logging and no clear answer to: am I getting better, and what should I do today?
Problem.text: People who want to look after their mental health usually start strong and stop after a week. Mood trackers collect data but don't explain it, meditation apps don't know how you feel today, and therapy is expensive with long waiting lists. The result is a lot of logging and no clear answer to: am I getting better, and what should I do today?
Problem.hmw: How might we help people understand their mental state in seconds and give them one small, useful action every day?

Research.label: 02 — RESEARCH
Research.name: Research
Research.finding: Main finding: people stopped because the app felt like homework, the charts didn’t tell them anything, and paid content appeared before any value.

Audience.name: Audience
Audience.intro: Who the site is for, what each group needs, and the page that answers it.

A check-in that takes seconds, not minutes.

personas.name: Investors & developers

To see how sleep, mood and stress connect.

personas.name: Public sector clients

Safe support and a clear route to a professional.

Journey map.label: 04 — JOURNEY MAP
Journey map.name: Journey map
Journey map.intro: What a visitor does, thinks and struggles with at each step, and the design decision that answers it.

rows.label: DESIGN RESPONSE
cells: Mood, sleep, stress and AI in one app
Value first, upgrade after real use

Hypotheses.label: 05 — HYPOTHESES
Hypotheses.name: Hypotheses
Hypotheses.intro: Eight hypotheses, each with its own metric, ordered by priority. Drawn as variants of one component: same structure, different bet.
items: One 0–100 score is easier to follow than separate mood, sleep and stress charts.
A short assessment at the start makes the first result feel personal.
3–4 suggested actions after each score turn logging into action.
A one-tap emoji check-in keeps daily logging under 30 seconds.
Clear AI framing, with a route to a real professional, makes people trust the chat.
Weekly chat use, support link taps
Smart reminders based on the user’s own patterns work better than fixed daily pings.
Optional voice input helps people who find it hard to put feelings into words.
Showing paid features after real use converts better than a paywall after onboarding.

Prioritisation.label: 06 — PRIORITISATION
Prioritisation.name: Prioritisation
Prioritisation.intro: Each hypothesis placed by expected impact and the effort to build it. The score went first even as a big bet: every other feature depends on it.

Visitor flow.label: 07 — VISITOR FLOW
Visitor flow.name: Visitor flow
Visitor flow.intro: The daily loop and the support path. Both end with one next step: an action, an exercise or a link to a professional.

Sitemap.label: 08 — SITEMAP
Sitemap.name: Sitemap
Sitemap.intro: Five tabs: Home, Practices, Journal and Profile, with Glow AI in the central button.

Wireframes to UI.label: 09 — WIREFRAMES TO UI
Wireframes to UI.name: Wireframes to UI
Wireframes to UI.intro: Low-fidelity layout first, agreed with the client, then the final interface.

Solution.label: 10 — SOLUTION
Solution.name: Solution
notes: Assessment
14 questions, one per screen, with a progress counter and a skip option on sensitive topics.
InnerGlow Score
One number from 0 to 100 with a plain-language label, and a history of what changed.
AI suggestions
3–4 actions after each score — mindfulness, activity, social, professional support — with time needed.
Mood check-in
One tap with 5 emoji states and an optional note. 12 seconds on average in testing.
AI companion
Text and voice chat with clear limits. Support contacts always sit in the chat header.
Trade-off
A single score can feel reductive, so details stay one tap away and every score has a label in words.

What we measure.label: 12 — WHAT WE MEASURE
What we measure.name: What we measure
What we measure.intro: Eight hypotheses across five stages of the journey. Targets were set before launch; the prototype test already gave a first signal for four of the five stages.
table: Weekly opens of score history; actions completed weekly
5 of 6 called actions the most useful part
Weekly chat use, support link taps
2 of 6 missed support contacts CHANGED THE DESIGN Moved into the chat header
Notification opt-out, share of voice entries, trial start, day-7 retention

Results.label: 13 — RESULTS
Results.name: Results
cols: Tested as a prototype

Moderated sessions with 6 people on Maze. 6 of 6 finished onboarding and understood their first score without help. The mood check-in took 12 seconds on average, and 5 of 6 said the suggested actions were the most useful part. Two people missed the support contacts, so they moved into the chat header.
What I would do next

In mental health products, tone matters as much as layout: “difficult day” instead of “negative” changed how people read the same chart. Next: test a shorter 5-question assessment, then track day-2 and day-7 retention and weekly suggested actions.

Problem.name: Problem
Problem.intro: JBC's clients are venue owners, operators and investors planning large, long-term projects. Before they get in touch, they check one thing: has this firm delivered a project like mine? The firm's experience was not presented in one clear place, so the answer was hard to find.
Problem.text: JBC's clients are venue owners, operators and investors planning large, long-term projects. Before they get in touch, they check one thing: has this firm delivered a project like mine? The firm's experience was not presented in one clear place, so the answer was hard to find.
Problem.hmw: How might we help visitors confirm JBC’s experience in one visit and make contacting the firm the obvious next step?

Problem.text: Thallo is still under construction, so there is no finished building to show. Companies looking for an office need to picture the space, understand what they can rent and decide if it is worth a viewing — all from renders and plans.

notes: One-page structure
The site has one job — viewing requests — so everything sits on one page.
Key facts row
Floors, completion, green features and access as short numbers.
Project highlights
Three stories with interior renders: premium offices, eco working and raised ceilings.
Six feature cards
Smart building, solar, raised floors, efficient HVAC, EV charging, architecture.
Floor specs
Nine floor tabs, each with indoor, outdoor and total area.
Trade-off
One long page keeps the path short but needs clear section titles.

What I would do next
When a building does not exist yet, clear numbers and good renders do most of the selling. Next: interactive floor plans, a construction progress section and a brochure download for an email.

pcela.title: Pcela Flower
pcela.intro: A flower shop where a gift for someone else is ordered on a phone in a few minutes.

Problem.label: 01 — PROBLEM
Problem.name: Problem
Problem.intro: Most people buy flowers in a hurry: a birthday, a date, an apology. They open the site on a phone and want to choose a bouquet, a time and an address in minutes. Many orders go to another person, sometimes anonymously — and the range is wide.
Problem.text: Most people buy flowers in a hurry: a birthday, a date, an apology. They open the site on a phone and want to choose a bouquet, a time and an address in minutes. Many orders go to another person, sometimes anonymously — and the range is wide.
Problem.hmw: How might we help someone find the right bouquet and send it to another person quickly, on a phone, without calling the shop?

Research.label: 02 — RESEARCH
Research.name: Research
Research.finding: Main finding: customers decide by photo and delivery time, not by descriptions. Most order for someone else and worry about timing and the recipient’s details.

Audience.label: 03 — AUDIENCE
Audience.name: Audience
Audience.intro: Who the site is for, what each group needs, and the page that answers it.

personas.name: Last-minute buyers
texts: Speed and a clear delivery time.

personas.name: Companies

Hypotheses.label: 05 — HYPOTHESES
Hypotheses.name: Hypotheses
Hypotheses.intro: Five hypotheses, each with its own metric. Drawn as variants of one component: same structure, different bet.
items: Three promises in the hero — 90-minute delivery, freshness, a gift — build trust faster than long text.
Catalogue clicks from the first screen
An online showcase and collections by bouquet type help visitors find a bouquet faster.
Showcase and collection clicks, time to first product
An order form built around “who is it for” reduces mistakes in recipient details.
Gift add-ons offered in the cart raise the average order value.
Share of orders with an add-on
Messengers, quick order and a callback catch people who prefer to talk.

Prioritisation.label: 06 — PRIORITISATION
Prioritisation.name: Prioritisation
Prioritisation.intro: Each hypothesis placed by expected impact and the effort to build it. The hero promises went first; the showcase and the order form were the big bets.

Solution.label: 10 — SOLUTION
Solution.name: Solution
notes: Three promises
Delivery in 90 minutes, a freshness guarantee, a gift box and bag from 10,000 ₽.
Online showcase
Ready bouquets delivered in 90 minutes, then bestsellers and categories: premium, mono, baskets, WOW sets.
Add-ons in the cart
Polaroid cards and CULTI / ’CAUSE fragrances offered right in the cart.
Order form
Contact, Telegram nickname, recipient, address, delivery date, anonymous delivery.
Quick contact
VK, WhatsApp, Telegram and Max, a call button, quick order and a callback.
Trade-off
A form and a manager instead of full checkout: flexible, but one manual step.

What I would do next
In flower e-commerce the photo sells and the form decides. Next: online payment in the cart and one delivery promise across the site.
